core: Definition of inflation as a general rise in the average level of prices over time
Purchasing power: inflation reduces what a given amount of money can buy
The measure: inflation rate as the rate of change in prices, tracked by indexes such as the Consumer Price Index
Causes: demand-pull, cost-push, and expectations — each stated factually, no policy positions
Who inflation hurts (savers, fixed incomes) and who it helps (borrowers), with an original example

claims.claim: Inflation is a general rise in the average level of prices over time.
Rising prices reduce purchasing power — what a given amount of money can buy.
The inflation rate is the rate of change in prices over a period, usually a year, and is commonly tracked through price indexes such as the Consumer Price Index.
Demand-pull inflation occurs when demand for goods and services grows faster than supply, pulling prices up.
Cost-push inflation occurs when increases in production costs, such as materials and wages, push up the prices of final goods and services.
Expectations that prices will keep rising can reinforce inflation, as workers demand higher wages and buyers speed up planned purchases.
Inflation generally harms savers and people on fixed incomes by eroding purchasing power, and can benefit borrowers because the real value of their debts shrinks over time.
Nominal amounts are stated before adjusting for inflation; real amounts are restated after removing inflation's effect (for example, real GDP is GDP adjusted for inflation).
Inflation is an important macroeconomic variable that influences prices, and firms consider it — along with interest rates — when building financial and operating plans.
The Federal Reserve's monetary policy goals, assigned by Congress, include stable prices.

positions: Demand-pull, cost-push, and expectations are the standard textbook drivers (OpenStax, Investopedia).
CFI notes the short- and medium-run causes remain contested among economists, with a consensus that long-run inflation is tied to changes in the money supply.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the three standard drivers factually and takes no position on which matters most or on policy; the money-supply view is acknowledged only as a contested long-run explanation in the evidence packet, not asserted in the lesson.
